text:
The girl did not have the courage to extricate herself from that tormenting situation: the entire Gianella family—Adolfo’s mother, father, uncles, and cousins—surrounded her, extolling the young man’s virtues, making plans for the future, showing themselves so certain, so delighted by that singularly happy marriage, that Loredana suffocated and remained silent. But it would have been impossible to find a man more incapable of understanding her than Adolfo, so much so that she, who was kind to everyone, was always irritated, nervous, and sorrowful with him.

Lately he had even wanted to read the letters she received from her friends, whom he did not trust at all; one morning, while he had gone to bid his fiancée good morning, the letter carrier arrived, and Adolfo seized the mail, opened a letter from a girl who was writing to Loredana from a town in the province, asked about the people mentioned in it, and ended by putting the letter in his pocket.

When Filippo arrived toward evening, the girl was still quivering all over with indignation and anger; she told her friend everything, even what she had kept silent until that day: Adolfo’s harassment, stinginess, insulting distrust, unreasonable jealousy, and presumption.

“I do not want him, I do not want him, I do not want him!” she exclaimed, her eyes flashing with rage. “Anything rather than this marriage! Never, never, never!”

Filippo had listened in silence, looking at the floor of red and white tiles and marking the rhythm of a march with his foot.

Suddenly he raised his head, grasped his friend’s hands, and asked:

“Would you come with me?”

The girl did not understand at once.

“Where?” she asked.

“Away, far away, out of Venice, forever!” Filippo pressed her.

“Run away? Run away with you?” she said in a low voice, already trembling without knowing why.

“Listen to me,” Filippo murmured.

He went as far as the threshold of the little sitting room, saw that Mama was intently reading a poorly bound book, and continued as he returned to Loredana:

“What we call friendship is nothing but love. Have you realized it?”

She remained rigid and motionless, her eyes wide open, and did not answer.

“I have realized it,” Filippo went on. “I know that I love you, I feel that I love you, I feel that we can be happy. I cannot marry you; understand me clearly, I cannot marry you because my whole family would cause us so many, so very many sorrows that, by comparison, what you have suffered until now would seem a joy to you. They are ignorant, stubborn, and ferocious.... But I offer you my love and my life all the same.... I too am tired; I too can no longer drag out this tormenting and useless existence. Tell me that you accept, and we shall be happy.... We shall leave at once....”

Loredana withdrew her hands from Filippo’s and rose to her feet: she took a few steps as though to leave the room, but stopped and leaned back against the wall; she was weeping in silence, and the tears ran down her cheeks.

Filippo approached her again. He was pale, and his voice trembled. He said:

“Are you offended?”

She shook her head.

“Then you are not in love with me, as I am with you?”

No answer came. Loredana looked at her friend through the veil of her tears. He took a step as though to move away, but the girl quickly, instinctively, stopped him with a gesture.

“Yes, I love you too,” she murmured in a low voice.

Filippo seized her around the waist and kissed her on the mouth.

“Think about it,” he said. “Think how very happy we shall be.... Mama will forgive you. She loves you too dearly to condemn you. She will understand that you had the right to live, to escape a dreadful future. You will know how to make her forgive you, will you not? For you know the way to reach Mama’s heart! Tell me that you accept, and we shall leave at once....”

She, still leaning against the wall, still motionless, her eyes full of tears, did not answer. But a peal of the doorbell made both her and Filippo start.

The girl hastily dried her eyes and ran into the little sitting room.

“It must be Adolfo,” she said to Mama. “I have a migraine, I do not want to see him, I am going to shut myself in my room!”

Mama sighed and raised her eyes to the ceiling. Loredana returned to Filippo and clasped his hands while he kissed her once more on the mouth.

“Think about it!” Filippo repeated.

She made a vague gesture and disappeared, to shut herself in her little room.

Adolfo Gianella was coming up the stairs, and Filippo, hearing his footsteps, was saying to Signora De Carolis:

“I am very sorry that the young lady is indisposed; I hope it is nothing....”

“Is she ill?” Adolfo asked as he arrived, greeting Filippo with a cold salutation and a sidelong glance. “Where was she last evening? She must have caught cold, or eaten something indigestible....”

Filippo left at once, and despite himself he said inwardly, laughing:

“You will soon have to eat something indigestible yourself!...”

That night he thought again about the idea of running away, which had flashed upon him so suddenly; and the more he thought about it, the better it seemed to him. Signora De Carolis would not have dared do anything against her adored daughter; Adolfo would have found consolation in the thought that a girl capable of running away with Count Vagli was unworthy of him.... In the end, the affair would have become known only to a few, and imperfectly, and it would have been diminished, pulverized, so to speak, in the classic gossip of Venice. Filippo found the honesty in his dishonesty; he loved Loredana; he felt that he would be faithful to her, that he would make her happy, that she would not suffer, and since it was absurd to speak of marriage because of the formidable opposition he would encounter in his family, running away—a prudent flight, without too much scandal, without commotion—would put an end to a situation that was unbearable for him and for his little friend.

The thought of Fausta also came to him; but in that period the unfortunate woman had fallen utterly in his eyes because of her strange humble behavior, which he could not understand at all. He thought regretfully of his mistress’s devotion: Fausta was not made to obey, to remain silent, to suffer; every woman has her own charm and her own destiny. Subservience had dimmed the beautiful flame of those sky-blue eyes and robbed her face of the complexion of fresh youth.
